title: Kuol's sisters stall shooting inquiry
article: A last-minute plea from a woman who recently escaped a Kenyan refugee camp stalled a fatality inquiry into the death of a Sudanese immigrant shot by a Calgary police officer two years ago.

The inquiry into the death of Deng Kuol -- set to begin Monday -- was adjourned until this morning after a last-ditch bid by two of Kuol's sisters to have legal counsel appear at the hearing on their behalf.
The surprise application was made by Martin Yak, a spokesman for the New Alberta Sudanese Community Association, and stopped the inquiry before it even began.
It also came eight months after the hearing dates were set, frustrating other parties including the province, which had witnesses already in place to testify Monday.
Yak said he was made aware of the hearing dates in January, but had only just managed to speak with Kuol's two sisters to get authorization to find a lawyer to represent them at the inquiry.

He was waiting on a letter from one of Kuol's sisters -- now living in Australia after more than 10 years in a Kenyan refugee camp -- that would allow him to hire a lawyer on their behalf and have them represented at the inquiry.
It prompted provincial court Judge Gerald Meagher to adjourn the inquiry, before witnesses could be called and before evidence could be heard.

"Our people are in refugee camps. These ladies were in camps in Kenya. They didn't have telephones for me to call them," Yak told the inquiry. "They have been on the move for the whole of this year. It wasn't easy for me to contact them."

Deng Fermino Kuol died from two bullet wounds in his neck after he was shot by Const. Ira Macumber on Oct. 25, 2003. The shooting happened after police were called to a disturbance in the 1700 block of 37th Street S.E.

The 34-year-old, who came to Calgary in 1997 after escaping wartorn Sudan, was intoxicated and allegedly attacked Macumber with a knife, slashing him in the arm before the officer responded in self-defence.

Macumber, a four-year member of the force, was cleared of wrongdoing following an investigation by the homicide unit and reviews by the Calgary Police Service's professional standards section and the Edmonton special crown prosecutor.
The inquiry will focus on several key issues, including the police service's policy on using deadly force. It will not apportion blame.

The province was set to begin Monday with Det. John Manahan, the police homicide unit lead investigator in the case. With Manahan set to leave for the Okanagan this morning on holiday, the delay has forced the province to shuffle its witness schedule.
Jo-Ann Burgess, counsel for the minister of justice and attorney general, fought against Monday's adjournment, saying Yak had ample time to prepare for the inquiry.

"Mr. Yak was first given notice of the inquiry in January . . . some eight months ago," she said. "We have some 18 witnesses scheduled to give evidence. There's a witness today from out of town. Counsel and various witnesses have rearranged vacation schedules to accommodate these dates."
But Yak said outside court that Kuol's sisters could not be reached until recently.

"They were in very remote areas where there were no facilities, even by sending a letter would have taken about six months. That is Africa. It wasn't easy for us to contact the sisters," he said. "They feel that it is necessary for the family to be represented."
Yak said the local Sudanese community is seeking "justice," adding the anger of two years ago has diminished.
